$$

$$

$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-4y &=-2 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x-4y=-2.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=4y-2,$ and the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=4y-2 \\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4y-2 \\ y\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=\begin{bmatrix}0.7 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.1 & 0.4\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.3 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & -0.2 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.1 & -0.6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-0.3 & 0.1 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.2 & -0.2 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.1 & 0.1 & -0.6 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}-3 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -6 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -6 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 3 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -15 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{15}{4}{x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+\frac{15}{4}{x}_{3}-6{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{9}{4}{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{9}{4}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{15}{4}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{4}{x}_{3}+\frac{15}{4}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 7{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{9}{28} \\ \frac{15}{28} \\ \frac{1}{7}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, after many elections, $\frac{1}{7}$ of the people will vote for the red party. Therefore, the number of people that will vote for the red party equals

$$
\frac{1}{7}\cdot 5.6\,\text{million}=0.8\,\text{million}.
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =1.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}-1\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=6,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{6}{-2}=-3.$

$$

Notice that if we divide the first equation by $23$ and the second equation by $10,$ we will get a $2y$ term in the first equation that can cancel with the $-2y$ term in the second equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}23x+46y &=690 && |\,÷23 \\ 10x-20y &=100 && |\,÷10\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=30 \\ x-2y &=10\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+\cancel{2y} & =30 \\ x-\cancel{2y} & =10 \\ (x+x) & =(30+10) \\ 2x & =40 \\ x & =20\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2y & =30 \\ (20)+2y & =30 \\ 2y & =30-20 \\ 2y & =10 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x-y=20-(5)=15.
$$

We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =1+{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \text{d}u & =2x\,\text{d}x \\ 2\,\text{d}u & =4x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=1+{x}^{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 2 \\ u & 1 & 5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{(1+{x}^{2})}\cdot 4x\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u & =2{\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{1}^{5} \\  & =2(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=6 \\ y+z &=5 \\ z &=3,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=3$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+(3)=5\,⟹\,y=5-3=2.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=2$ and $z=3$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(2)+(3)=6\,⟹\,x=6-5=1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=1,y=2$ and $z=3.$
